Yes, so proving factorization is in P doesn't prove that P=NP.

Integer factorization is in NP though (it's just not proven to be NP-hard). So proving that you can't factorize in polynomial time would prove that P!=NP.
Integer factorization is not known to be NP Complete.
It would prove P!=NP...

> this theorem simply removes the theoretical possibility that worst-case hard instances exist that resist $L_N[1/3]$ algorithms.

I don't think this theorem proves this. This would be an enormously huge deal, because it would show that factoring is not polynomial. The paper would state that front and center, in the abstract, in the title, and about 10 more times on the first two pages.

I think the paper just says that what was known empirically in the past (that factorization can be done with an algorithm in the L_N[1/3, O(1)] class), is now proven formally. It does not establish a lower bound.

children.author: amelius
simiones
children.text: The exponent is 105 * n^1/3 * (log n)^2/3 for the proven deterministic algorithm (this is what L[1/3, 105] apparently means). Note that the best known probabilistic algorithm, much older than this, was 1.923 * n^1/3 * (log n)^2/3 (this was L[1/3, 1.923]). This older algorithm is thus ~exp(103) times faster than the newly proven one, hence why this has no cryptographic impact. Note that n here is the bit size of the number you are trying to factor.
